## How To Use This Script

Use this page when you want a fuller spoken version of the ITS deck rather than cue cards.

- Keep the [Interrupted Time Series note](../notes/other-methods/interrupted-time-series.qmd) open for equations, code, and references.
- Allow about one minute per content slide, with extra time for the counterfactual and controlled-ITS slides.
- Trim examples rather than rushing the distinction between an estimated break and a causal effect.
- Use the two labs after the deck so learners first understand the design problem and then see how the models behave.

## Slide-By-Slide Script

### Title Slide

Today we are looking at interrupted time series as a way to evaluate an intervention introduced at a known time. The method is attractive because it uses the full trajectory rather than one observation before and one after. But that extra structure does not make causality automatic. The central question throughout the session is whether the no-policy trajectory is credible and whether another event could have generated the same break.

### Session Promise

The promise of the session is simple: by the end, you should be able to separate what the model estimates from what the design allows you to claim. We will start with the missing counterfactual, specify the expected impact shape, account for time-series structure, and then confront the threats that matter most—especially concurrent shocks and changes in measurement.

### 20-Minute Arc

The sequence moves from identification to estimation and back to identification. We first ask why repeated observations improve on pre/post comparison. We then map substantive expectations into level and trend terms. After that we handle seasonality and autocorrelation. The final part asks whether the observed break is really attributable to the intervention and shows how a credible comparison series can help.

### A Pre/Post Difference Has No Trajectory

A before-and-after average compresses the series so aggressively that it throws away the information ITS is meant to use. If admissions were already rising, the post-policy average may be higher even when the policy helped. If the policy starts at a seasonal peak, the post average may fall simply because the calendar moved on. We need the pre-policy path because it tells us what direction the outcome was already moving and how it usually fluctuated.

### ITS Projects the Pre-Policy Path Forward

The untreated counterfactual in an uncontrolled ITS is the projected continuation of the pre-policy trajectory. The observed post-policy data tell us what happened with the intervention; the projected line represents what the model says would have happened without it. The gap is the estimated effect. Emphasize that the orange line is an estimate, not an observed untreated city. Its causal meaning depends on whether the pre-policy model remains credible after the intervention date.

### The Expected Impact Shape Belongs in the Design

Interventions do not all act in the same way. A ban may produce an immediate level change. A programme that builds capacity may change the trend gradually. Some interventions plausibly do both. Others create a temporary disruption and then fade. These shapes should come from implementation knowledge and the proposed mechanism. Choosing one after looking at the graph turns the analysis into a search for the most favourable break.

### Segmented Regression Separates Level and Trend Changes

Walk through the four central terms. The intercept and time trend describe the pre-intervention trajectory. The intervention indicator captures the discontinuity at the first intervention observation. Time after the intervention captures how the slope changes from that point onward. The post-policy slope is therefore the old slope plus the slope change. Seasonality and the error structure sit alongside these terms because repeated observations are rarely independent or season-free.

### Post-Intervention Time Must Start at Zero

This is a small coding choice with a large interpretive consequence. If time after intervention is zero at the first treated observation, the intervention coefficient is the immediate level change at that moment. If we instead multiply calendar time by the intervention indicator, the fitted line can be identical but the intervention coefficient is shifted to an extrapolated and usually meaningless time origin. The mechanics lab demonstrates this directly by fitting both parameterizations and comparing their fitted values and coefficients.

### The Effect Changes With the Horizon

When both the level and trend change, there is no single effect that applies to every post-policy month. The immediate effect is the level-change coefficient. Twelve months later, the trend change has accumulated for twelve periods. The confidence interval must use the covariance between the two coefficients as well as their separate variances. Reporting one coefficient as “the policy effect” misses this dynamic structure.

### Plot the Series Before Estimating

The raw plot is the first diagnostic, not a decorative result. Look for the baseline trend, repeated seasonal movement, isolated outliers, missing periods, and any visible transition around implementation. Also ask whether the proposed impact shape looks remotely compatible with the data. If the series contains a structural break long before the policy, a single linear pre-trend may already be implausible.

### Seasonality Belongs in the Mean Model

Monthly health outcomes often have strong annual cycles. If a policy begins in January, a winter peak can be mistaken for a policy jump or decline. Fourier terms give us a compact way to represent a smooth annual cycle; month indicators are another transparent option. The choice should reflect how the outcome behaves. Omitting seasonality does not merely make the plot untidy—it can distort the intervention terms and leave strong residual structure.

### Autocorrelation Belongs in the Error Model

After accounting for the expected mean trajectory, adjacent residuals may still be correlated. Ordinary least squares treats them as independent, so its uncertainty can be misleading. In the simulation we know the errors follow an AR(1) process, making AR(1) generalized least squares a sensible model. In real work we would inspect residual time plots, ACF and PACF patterns, and compare plausible structures rather than assuming AR(1) by habit.

### A Concurrent Shock Can Mimic the Policy

This is the central causal threat in an uncontrolled ITS. If a strike, recession, eligibility change, or second policy begins on the same date, segmented regression cannot decide which event caused the break. Better standard errors do not help because this is not an uncertainty problem; it is an identification problem. A dated context timeline and substantive investigation are therefore part of the analysis.

### Measurement Must Not Break With the Policy

The outcome has to mean the same thing across the interruption. Check definitions, denominators, system coverage, coding practices, and population composition. A new reporting system introduced with a policy may produce a clean and precisely estimated level change, but that does not make it a policy effect. A comparison series also cannot repair a measurement change that affects only the treated series.

### Timing Should Follow Implementation, Not Significance

Formal launch dates are not always the correct impact dates. People may anticipate a rule, implementation may phase in, or effects may take time to emerge. Represent those features when implementation evidence supports them. What we should not do is move the date or try many lags until a significant estimate appears. The timing model should describe delivery, not optimize the result.

### A Credible Control Can Remove Shared Shocks

A controlled ITS compares the change in the treated series with the contemporaneous change in an unexposed series. If both series experience the same unrelated shock, the common change can be separated from the treated-versus-control contrast. The control is only helpful when it is measured comparably, tracks a plausible untreated process, and is not itself affected by the intervention. Show both the treated series alone and the controlled contrast so the design remains inspectable.

### Diagnostics Are Part of the Causal Argument

Diagnostics should map onto named concerns. Compare a few plausible trend forms when curvature is substantively possible. Inspect residual dependence and seasonal structure. Represent a known transition window. Test a negative-control outcome or comparison series when available. Sensitivity analysis is strongest when each alternative answers a design question; an unrestricted menu encourages specification search and makes the conclusion harder to interpret.

### Familiar Shortcuts Create Predictable Failures

Three shortcuts recur. First, two observations do not make an interrupted time series because there is no trajectory to estimate. Second, convenient post-time coding can preserve fitted values while destroying the coefficient interpretation. Third, fixing autocorrelation does not eliminate a concurrent event. These failures look different in code, but all come from treating the estimator as if it supplied the design.

### Report the Trajectory, Not Just Coefficients

A defensible report tells the reader what was interrupted, when, and why that impact shape was expected. It documents the observation frequency, outcome definition, denominator, and measurement process. It shows the observed, fitted, and no-policy trajectories, then reports immediate and horizon-specific effects with uncertainty. Finally, it states the remaining concurrent-event and measurement threats so the causal conclusion is proportionate to the evidence.

### The Labs Move From Mechanics to Design

The first lab makes the segmented-regression machinery transparent. Learners construct the variables, see the coding trap, model autocorrelation, and calculate horizon effects. The second lab turns to identification. It compares a valid case, an omitted-seasonality specification, a shared concurrent shock, and a treated-only measurement break. The controlled model can address the shared shock, but it cannot tell a real policy effect from a treated-only measurement discontinuity.

### Sources

This slide collects the references supporting the deck. It does not need a spoken walkthrough; use it to point learners to the applied tutorial, controlled-ITS guidance, parameterization warning, segmented-regression introduction, and risk-of-bias framework.

### The Design Makes the Break Causal

Close with the practical sequence. Plot the series. Specify the timing and expected impact shape from implementation knowledge. Model seasonality and serial dependence. Then ask whether another event, reporting change, or population shift could have produced the same result. A significant break is an estimate. It becomes a causal claim only when the counterfactual and the surrounding design are credible.
